Spot artifacts mark tappable regions in text as [[id|text]]. Run python scripts/build_content.py && python scripts/validate_content.py after editing.

simulations.title: Who really sent this?
intro: Scammers borrow names you trust. The address behind the name is what counts.
Read the domain from right to left: the part just before .com or .in is who it's really from.
Seven quick rounds. Take your time.

rounds.prompt: Which address is NovaCorp's real IT helpdesk?

options.text: helpdesk@novacorp.com
helpdesk@novac0rp.com
options.note: A zero instead of the letter o.

rounds.explain: One character is all it takes. Lookalike domains swap letters for numbers or similar letters.

rounds.prompt: Which sign-in page really belongs to NovaCorp?

options.text: https://novacorp.com.sso-check.in/login
options.note: The real domain is sso-check.in; novacorp.com is just a prefix.

options.text: https://sso.novacorp.com/login

rounds.explain: Read right to left: the domain is the part just before the first single slash. Anything before it can be made up.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

body: [[deadline|Your EPF nomination will be cancelled at 6 PM today]] unless you confirm your details.

regions.label: Sender address
regions.why: novacorp-benefits.com isn't novacorp.com. Anyone can register a domain like that.

regions.label: Same-day deadline
regions.why: A hard deadline is there to rush you past checking.

regions.label: Link
regions.why: It goes to nova-hr-portal.in, not hr.novacorp.com.

regions.label: Signature
regions.why: A normal sign-off. Scams copy these, so it proves nothing either way.

rounds.explain: Three flags: a lookalike sender, a same-day deadline and a link that leaves NovaCorp.

rounds.prompt: Both say "Elena Vance". Which one is really our CEO?

options.text: Elena Vance <elena.vance.novacorp@gmail.com>
options.note: A free webmail address with the company name stuck on.

options.text: Elena Vance <elena.vance@novacorp.com>

rounds.explain: Anyone can type any display name. Look at the address behind it.

rounds.prompt: BrightClean is a long-standing vendor. Which address is theirs?

options.text: accounts@brightclean.in
accounts@brightclean-services.in
options.note: An extra word makes a different domain owned by someone else.

rounds.explain: Extra words, hyphens or a new ending (.co instead of .com) make a completely different domain.

rounds.prompt: Sort your inbox: safe to deal with, or report?

items.label: Planned VPN maintenance Saturday
items.why: The real IT address, and it asks you for nothing.

items.label: Your salary slip (attached .html)
items.why: .co isn't .com, and payslips are never .html files.

items.label: Priya shared "Team rota.xlsx"
items.why: drive.novacorp.com is NovaCorp's own file service.

items.label: Quick favour, are you at your desk?
items.why: A lookalike domain opening with a vague favour: a classic first step of CEO fraud.

rounds.explain: Check the domain on every email, even the friendly ones.

rounds.prompt: An email from accounts@brightclean.in (the real address) asks you to update their bank details. What's the right check?

options.text: Call BrightClean on the number in their contract
Reply to the email and ask them to confirm
Call the phone number in the email's signature
Nothing: the address is correct, so it's safe

rounds.explain: Real addresses get hacked. When an email changes money or access, confirm through a channel you already had.

recap: Read the domain right to left: the part just before .com or .in is who it's from.
A familiar display name means nothing; check the address behind it.
When an email changes money or access, confirm through a channel you already know.

sources.title: Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks
Guidelines on Information Security Practices for Government Entities

simulations.title: Where does this link really go?
intro: A link's words can say anything. The address underneath decides where you land.
On a laptop, hover over it. On a phone, press and hold to preview it.
QR codes are links too, just harder to read. Let's practise.

rounds.prompt: Which link really opens NovaCorp's HR portal?

options.text: https://hr.novacorp.com/payslips
https://hr-novacorp.com/payslips
options.note: The hyphen makes hr-novacorp.com, a different domain.

rounds.explain: A dot keeps you inside novacorp.com. A hyphen creates a new domain that anyone could own.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this text message.

art.text: [[track|Parcel NP-4471]] is on hold. [[fee|Pay a ₹25 redelivery fee]] within [[time|2 hours]] or it goes back:

regions.label: Sender
regions.why: Couriers text from short sender IDs, not a random mobile number.

regions.label: Small fee
regions.why: A tiny fee gets your card details. The parcel is the bait.

regions.label: 2-hour limit
regions.why: Short deadlines stop you checking.

regions.label: Link
regions.why: A cheap .top domain that isn't the courier's site.

regions.label: Tracking number
regions.why: Tracking numbers look official but are easy to make up. Not a flag on its own.

rounds.explain: If you're expecting a parcel, open the courier's app or website yourself and check there.

rounds.prompt: Which sign-in address is safe to use?

options.text: https://novacorp.com.secure-login.net/sso
https://sso.novacorp.com

rounds.explain: The safest sign-in is one you open yourself from a bookmark or by typing it.

rounds.prompt: A poster in the lobby says "Scan for free guest Wi-Fi". The QR code is a sticker on top of the print. What do you do?

options.text: Ask reception for the guest Wi-Fi details and tell them about the sticker
Scan it: it's in our own lobby
Scan it, but don't type a password
Take a photo to scan later at home

rounds.explain: A sticker over a printed QR code is a common trick. Get the details from a person you trust instead.

rounds.prompt: Safe to open, or report?

items.label: drive.novacorp.com/share/team-rota
items.why: NovaCorp's own file service, shared by a colleague you were expecting.

items.label: novacorp-drive.share-docs.net
items.why: The real domain is share-docs.net, plus a scare.

items.label: hr.novacorp.com/onboarding
items.why: The company's own HR portal, from the real HR address.

items.label: bit.ly/nova-bonus-2026
items.why: A short link hides where it goes, and surprise bonuses are classic bait.

rounds.explain: When a link hides its destination or leaves novacorp.com, don't sign in there.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

body: [[quota|Your mailbox is 99% full and new mail will bounce today.]]

regions.label: Sender address
regions.why: A .click domain, not novacorp.com.

regions.label: Bounce warning
regions.why: A scare with a same-day deadline.

regions.label: Upgrade link
regions.why: It opens a sign-in page on novamail-upgrade.click.

regions.label: Mailbox size
regions.why: Just a number; it doesn't tell you anything either way.

rounds.explain: Storage warnings are a favourite way to steal passwords. IT would never send you to a sign-in page off our domain.

recap: Hover, or press and hold on a phone, to see a link's real address before you tap.
QR codes are links you can't read: check the preview, and prefer the address you know.
Sign in only by opening the site yourself, never from a link in a message.

sources.title: Guidelines on Information Security Practices for Government Entities

simulations.title: Think before you open
intro: A file can do things a message can't, like run code on your laptop.
Unexpected attachments get checked first, even from people you know.
And no document needs macros just so you can read it.

rounds.prompt: Open it, or report it?

items.label: Invoice_4471.html
items.why: An .html "invoice" opens a fake sign-in page.

items.label: Q3_targets.xlsx
items.detail: From priya@novacorp.com, which you asked for
items.why: Expected, from a real colleague, in a normal format.

items.label: Contract_Final.docm
items.detail: "URGENT" from a vendor you've never heard of
items.why: .docm files carry macros. Unknown sender plus urgency: don't open.

items.label: Payslip_Oct.pdf.exe
items.why: The real ending is .exe, a program pretending to be a PDF.

items.label: Meeting_notes.pdf
items.why: Expected follow-up from a colleague, in a normal format.

rounds.explain: Check who sent it, whether you expected it, and the file's real ending.

rounds.prompt: A document opens with a yellow bar: "Enable editing", then "Enable content to view this document". What do you do?

options.text: Close it and report it to IT
Enable content: it came from a colleague
Enable editing but not content
Forward it to someone else to try

rounds.explain: Enabling content runs macros. A real document doesn't need that just to be read.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

body: [[threat|Legal action will begin in 24 hours]] unless the attached invoice is paid.

regions.label: Sender address
regions.why: supp1ies uses the number 1 instead of the letter l.

regions.label: Legal threat
regions.why: Threats with a deadline are there to scare you into opening.

regions.label: Zip attachment
regions.why: Zip files are often used to sneak harmful files past filters.

regions.label: Reference number
regions.why: Easy to fake, but not a warning sign on its own.

rounds.explain: Unknown sender, a threat and a zipped attachment: report it without opening anything.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this chat.

msgs: Your VPN client is out of date. [[file|Run Fix_VPN.exe]] from the link below.
[[rush|Please do it before 5 PM or you'll lose access.]]

regions.label: External account
regions.why: The real Dev is inside the NovaCorp workspace, not external.

regions.label: .exe file
regions.why: IT pushes updates centrally. Nobody should ask you to run a program from chat.

regions.label: Deadline
regions.why: Pressure again, so you don't stop and check.

regions.label: Friendly greeting
regions.why: Normal chat. Scams are friendly too, so it proves nothing.

rounds.explain: Check with the real Dev at the helpdesk (ext. 4357) before running anything.

rounds.prompt: An email from "HR" you weren't expecting has "Bonus_list.xlsm" attached. What's the right check?

options.text: Ask HR about it on NovaChat or by phone before opening
Open it on your phone instead of your laptop
Reply to the email and ask if it's real
Open it, then delete it if it looks odd

rounds.explain: Check unexpected files through a different channel. Replying goes straight back to the scammer.

rounds.prompt: You opened an attachment and a window flashed up and vanished. What now?

options.text: Tell IT straight away on ext. 4357 and stop using the laptop
Restart the laptop and carry on
Delete the email and say nothing
Run a quick antivirus scan and carry on

rounds.explain: Fast reports limit the damage. IT would much rather hear about a false alarm than find out too late.

recap: Unexpected attachment? Check with the sender through another channel before opening.
Never enable macros or content just to view a document.
If you've opened something suspicious, tell IT straight away. Quick reports limit the damage.

sources.title: Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks
Guidelines on Information Security Practices for Government Entities

simulations.title: Who's on the line?
intro: A confident voice and the right jargon can make anyone sound official.
Caller ID can be faked, and voices can be cloned from public videos.
Your best move is almost always the same: hang up and call back on a number you look up yourself.

rounds.prompt: Your desk phone rings. Choose what to say.

say: Hi, this is Arun from NovaCorp IT. We've spotted strange sign-ins on your account.
I need to install a support tool on your laptop to clean it up. Can you open a website for me?

choices.text: Sure, which website?
What's the ticket number?
I'll hang up and call the helpdesk on 4357.
choices.why: Calling back on the number you know is exactly right. Real IT won't mind.

say: There's no time for a ticket, your account is being used right now!
Just open the site and I'll do the rest.

choices.text: Okay, okay, which site?
Then I'll call the helpdesk on 4357 myself.
choices.why: Dodging the ticket question and adding pressure are big warning signs. Calling back was right.

say: Go to nova-remote-help.com and click Download. Then read me the number on screen.

choices.text: Download it and read out the number
choices.why: That remote tool would give the caller full control of your laptop.

choices.text: Actually, I'll call the helpdesk first.
choices.why: Good recovery. Stopping late is still far better than not stopping.

rounds.explain: Real IT raises a ticket and never minds you calling back on ext. 4357.

rounds.prompt: On a call, is it fine to carry on, or a reason to hang up and check?

items.label: "I'm calling about ticket #4471 you raised this morning."
items.why: A ticket you really raised, from the known helpdesk number.

items.label: "Read me the code we just texted you."
items.why: Nobody legitimate asks for your one-time code.

items.label: "Don't tell your manager, it's confidential."
items.why: Secrecy is a manipulation tactic. Real processes don't need it.

items.label: "Can I call you back on your desk number?"
items.why: Offering to call back on a known number is what genuine callers do.

rounds.explain: Codes, secrecy and pressure on a call mean: hang up and check.

rounds.prompt: Your mobile rings. It says "NovaBank". Choose what to say.

say: This is the NovaBank fraud team. A payment of ₹49,999 is pending on your card.
To block it, I'll send you a code. Please read it back to me.

choices.text: Okay, I've got the code. It's...
choices.why: That code approves the payment or a new device. The 'fraud team' was the fraudster.

choices.text: I'll hang up and call the number on the back of my card.
choices.why: Exactly right. The number on your card always reaches the real bank.

choices.text: How do I know you're really the bank?

say: I can see your name and the last four digits of your card. Isn't that enough?
Quickly, the payment goes through in two minutes.

choices.text: Fine, here's the code.
choices.why: Personal details are easy to buy. Knowing them proves nothing.

choices.text: I'll call the number on my card now.
choices.why: Right. A real bank is happy for you to call back.

rounds.explain: Banks never ask you to read out a code. The displayed name and number can be faked.

rounds.prompt: A caller says they're from the CFO's office and need the vendor list in the next ten minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll call back, then ring the CFO's office on the directory number
Send it: the CFO's office is senior
Ask them to email you from any address
Send only half the list

rounds.explain: Seniority and a deadline are pressure, not proof. The directory number is.

rounds.prompt: The meeting-room phone rings. The voice sounds just like our CEO.

say: It's Elena. I'm about to board a flight. I need a payment of ₹18,50,000 sent to our new legal partner now.

choices.text: Of course. Send me the details.
choices.why: Voices can be cloned. A personal 'authorisation' on a call skips every check.

choices.text: I'll raise it in the finance portal and confirm with you on your directory number.
choices.why: The process and a call-back protect you even if the voice is real.

choices.text: Can you tell me about this morning's all-hands?

say: I don't have time for quizzes! The deal closes in an hour.

choices.text: Sorry. I'll send it now.
choices.why: Dodging a simple question is a strong sign it isn't her.

choices.text: Then I'll call you back on your directory number.
choices.why: Right. Anyone can be impersonated; the directory number can't.

rounds.explain: Big payments always go through the finance portal, whoever is asking.

recap: Caller ID can be faked; a familiar number or voice isn't proof.
Never share one-time codes or passwords on a call, whoever asks.
Hang up and call back on a number you look up yourself.

sources.title: Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks
Guidelines on Information Security Practices for Government Entities

simulations.title: Texts and chats
intro: Texts and chats feel personal, which is exactly why scammers like them.
A new number, an External label or a prize you never entered should all make you pause.
Six rounds. Let's go.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this text.

art.text: [[greet|Dear customer]], your [[kyc|KYC expires today]]. [[block|Your account will be blocked]]. Update now:

regions.label: Sender number
regions.why: Banks text from short sender IDs, not a personal mobile number.

regions.label: Generic greeting
regions.why: Your bank knows your name.

regions.label: KYC deadline
regions.why: KYC updates are never a same-day emergency by text.

regions.label: Block threat
regions.why: Threats are there to rush you.

regions.label: Link
regions.why: Not the bank's real website. Use the official app instead.

rounds.explain: For anything about your bank account, open the bank's official app or call the number on your card.

rounds.prompt: Safe, or report?

items.label: "Hi, it's Hale. New number. Buy 5 gift cards for a client, I'll pay you back."
items.why: New number, gift cards and a favour: classic CEO-fraud recipe.

items.label: "Lunch at 1? Canteen has biryani today."
items.why: A real colleague inside the NovaCorp workspace, asking for nothing risky.

items.label: "You won ₹50,000 in NovaCorp's anniversary draw! Claim here."
items.why: You can't win a draw you never entered.

items.label: "Your NovaCorp SSO code is 482913. Never share it."
items.why: You asked for this code a moment ago. Use it, and don't share it.

rounds.explain: Ask: did I expect this, and does it want money, codes or a click?

rounds.prompt: Which NovaChat account is really Priya from HR?

options.text: @priya.sharrna · External
options.note: r and n together look like m, and it's an external account.

options.text: @priya.sharma · NovaCorp

rounds.explain: Squint-alike letters (rn for m) are a favourite trick. The External label gives it away.

rounds.prompt: A WhatsApp message from a new number says it's your manager and asks you to buy gift cards for a client urgently. What do you do?

options.text: Call your manager on their usual number, or ask them in person
Reply asking them to prove who they are
Buy one card first to be safe
Ignore it and tell nobody

rounds.explain: Check through a channel you already trust. Replying keeps you talking to the scammer, and telling IT helps colleagues too.

rounds.prompt: You are expecting a parcel. A text says delivery failed and gives a link to reschedule. What's the safest move?

options.text: Open the courier's official app or type their website yourself
Tap the link, since you are expecting a parcel
Reply with your address
Call the number in the text

rounds.explain: Scammers send these to everyone, knowing some people are expecting parcels.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this chat.

msgs: We're moving your account to a new server tonight.
[[code|Send me the 6-digit code you get on your phone]] [[quiet|and keep this between us so it doesn't slow the migration]].

regions.label: External label
regions.why: The real IT team is inside the NovaCorp workspace.

regions.label: Asks for your code
regions.why: A code proves you are you. Whoever has it can log in as you.

regions.label: Keep it quiet
regions.why: Secrecy stops you asking someone who'd spot the scam.

regions.label: Friendly hello
regions.why: Normal chat. Not a warning sign on its own.

rounds.explain: Report the account in NovaChat and tell IT on ext. 4357.

recap: New number claiming to be someone you know? Check with them on their usual number or in person.
Texts with tiny fees, prizes or account threats are bait; go to the official app yourself.
Look for External and Not-in-contacts labels before you trust a chat.

sources.title: Guidelines on Information Security Practices for Government Entities

simulations.title: Codes and sign-in prompts
intro: Two-step sign-in stops most account takeovers, as long as you don't hand the second step over.
Approve a prompt only if you started that sign-in, just now.
And a one-time code is like a key: nobody legitimate will ask for it.

rounds.prompt: Four sign-in prompts arrive on your phone. Decide each one.

prompts.context: You've just typed your password on your laptop.
prompts.why: You started this sign-in a moment ago, from the office.
You didn't start it. Someone has your password: deny, report and change it.

prompts.context: The fifth prompt in two minutes. You haven't tried to sign in.
prompts.why: Prompt bombing tries to wear you down until you tap Approve.

prompts.context: You just tapped Sign in on NovaMail on your phone.
prompts.why: Your own sign-in, just now. Approving is right.

rounds.explain: Only you know whether you started a sign-in. If you didn't, deny it and report it.

rounds.prompt: Your mobile rings.

say: Hi, IT here. We're resetting your two-step sign-in after an incident.
You'll get a code by text in a second. Read it to me so I can finish the reset.

choices.text: Okay, it's...
choices.why: With your password and that code, the caller is now in your account.

choices.text: IT never asks for codes. I'll call the helpdesk on 4357.
choices.why: Exactly. Even a number that ends in 4357 can be faked.

choices.text: Why do you need my code?

say: It links your account to the new system. Everyone's doing it today.
If you don't, you'll be locked out for the week.

choices.text: Fine, here's the code.
choices.why: 'Everyone's doing it' and a lock-out threat are pressure, not reasons.

choices.text: I'll check with the helpdesk first.
choices.why: Right. A real reset never needs your code read out.

rounds.explain: Your code is only ever typed into a sign-in page you opened yourself.

rounds.prompt: A colleague's phone has died. They ask you to approve a sign-in prompt for them on your phone. What do you suggest?

options.text: Ask the IT helpdesk to help them sign in another way
Approve it: you can see them at their desk
Give them your password for today
Approve it, then tell IT later

rounds.explain: Sign-in factors belong to one person. IT has safe ways to help someone without a phone.

rounds.prompt: Fine to do, or a reason to stop?

items.label: Typing your code into sso.novacorp.com, which you opened yourself
items.why: That's exactly where a code belongs.

items.label: "Reply to this text with the code to confirm your identity"
items.why: Codes are never sent back by reply.

items.label: Approving a prompt that shows the number you see on your laptop
items.why: Number matching confirms it's your own sign-in.

items.label: "Read the code to our agent to stop the account lock"
items.why: Lock-out threats plus a code request: a takeover attempt.

rounds.explain: Codes go into pages you opened, never to people.

rounds.prompt: Two more prompts. Decide each one.

prompts.context: You're in a meeting and haven't touched your laptop. It asks you to enter 47.
prompts.why: You didn't start this, even if it looks local. Deny and report.

prompts.context: Your laptop is showing 62 after you signed in. The prompt asks for 62.
prompts.why: Your sign-in, and the numbers match.

rounds.explain: A nearby location doesn't make a prompt yours. Only starting it yourself does.

rounds.prompt: You tapped Approve on a prompt by mistake. What now?

options.text: Tell IT straight away and change your password
Wait and see if anything happens
Deny the next prompt and forget it
Turn your phone off for an hour

rounds.explain: Quick action can lock the attacker out before they do anything. IT won't blame you for reporting.

recap: Approve a sign-in only if you started it, just now.
A one-time code is like a key: nobody legitimate will ask you for it.
Approved one by mistake? Tell IT straight away and change your password.

sources.title: Multi-factor authentication for your corporate online services

simulations.title: Desks, devices and paper
intro: Not every attack comes through a screen. Some are left on a desk or dropped in the car park.
Found devices, unlocked screens and stray printouts are all ways in.
Five quick situations around the office.

rounds.prompt: Rex has found something in the car park.
lines: Look, a USB drive! It says 'Salary_Revisions'.
Shall we plug it into the spare laptop and see whose it is?

options.text: Don't plug it in anywhere. Hand it to IT.
Plug it into the spare laptop, it's not connected to much
Drop it at reception's lost and found
Bin it so nobody else plugs it in

rounds.explain: A found drive can run code the moment it's connected, even on a 'spare' laptop. IT can check it safely.

rounds.prompt: Walking past a colleague's empty desk, tap every risk you see.

art.desc: A [[note|sticky note on the monitor: 'VPN: Monsoon@2026']], an [[screen|unlocked screen showing the payroll sheet]], a [[papers|printout marked CONFIDENTIAL]], a [[mug|NovaCorp coffee mug]] and a [[plant|small desk plant]].

regions.label: Password on a note
regions.why: Anyone walking past can read and use it.

regions.label: Unlocked screen
regions.why: Anyone could read or send as the owner.

regions.label: Confidential printout
regions.why: Confidential paper shouldn't sit on an empty desk.

regions.label: Coffee mug
regions.why: Just a mug.

regions.label: Desk plant
regions.why: Just a plant.

rounds.explain: Lock the screen for them (Windows + L), and tell them and IT so the password gets changed.

rounds.prompt: Pages titled 'Q3 salary bands: CONFIDENTIAL' have sat in the printer tray for an hour. The cover sheet says Priya, HR. What do you do?

options.text: Take them straight to Priya
Put them in the normal bin
Leave them: they aren't yours
Read them to see who they're for

rounds.explain: Return confidential paper to its owner, or use the shredder. The normal bin isn't private.

rounds.prompt: Good habit, or a risk to report?

items.label: Pressing Windows + L before a meeting
items.why: Two seconds, and nobody can use the laptop.

items.label: Laptop left unlocked in the café while ordering
items.why: Anyone can read or send from it while he's away.

items.label: Old payslips go in the shredder
items.why: Shredding is the right way to throw away personal data.

items.label: Customer list printout in the regular bin
items.why: Bins get emptied by people who shouldn't read it.

rounds.explain: Lock screens, shred paper, keep devices with you.

rounds.prompt: At reception, a visitor is handing out freebies.
lines: Free branded USB chargers from our company! A gift for your team.
Just plug them into your laptops, they're super fast.

options.text: Say thanks, don't plug them in, and pass them to IT to check
Take one and try it on your laptop
Hand them out to the team
Keep them in your drawer for later

rounds.explain: Unknown USB devices, even 'chargers', can contain hidden hardware. IT decides what gets plugged in.

recap: Never plug in a device you didn't get from IT.
Lock your screen every time you step away: Windows + L.
Confidential paper goes to its owner or the shredder, never the bin.

sources.title: Guidelines on Information Security Practices for Government Entities

simulations.title: Doors and visitors
intro: Holding a door open is polite, and attackers count on it.
Everyone signs in at reception or shows a badge, even with their hands full.
But genuine visitors deserve help too. Let's find the balance.

rounds.prompt: At the side door, someone with boxes calls out to you.
lines: Morning! Big delivery for the third floor.
My hands are full. Could you tap your badge and hold the door?

options.text: Point him to reception to sign in
Badge him in and hold the door
Badge him in but walk with him
Walk away without a word

rounds.explain: Reception is the one checkpoint for visitors. Pointing him there is polite and safe.

rounds.prompt: Outside the server room, a contractor stops you.
lines: Hi, I'm from CoolAir, here to service the AC.
Ada said it's fine, she's just busy. Can you let me in?

options.text: Ask him to wait while you check with Ada
Let him in: he named Ada
Let him in, and stay with him
Tell him to come back tomorrow

rounds.explain: Check 'X said it's fine' with X, not with the visitor. Ada is right inside.

rounds.prompt: In the lobby, someone with a new badge waves.
lines: Hi! I'm Kabir, I start in Finance today.
Mira signed me in. Could you point me to the HR room?

options.text: Show him the way to HR
Call Security on him
Refuse: you don't know him
Tell him to wait until someone else comes

rounds.explain: He has a badge, Mira signed him in, and he only wants directions. Helping genuine people is part of security too.

rounds.prompt: Someone in a NovaCorp T-shirt, with no badge, is walking around the open office looking at desks. What do you do?

options.text: Politely ask who they're looking for, and walk them to reception
Ignore them: the T-shirt shows they work here
Shout for Security straight away
Follow them quietly to see where they go

rounds.explain: A friendly question solves most of these. Reception can check and issue a badge.

rounds.prompt: Fine, or a reason to step in?

items.label: Visitor wearing a visitor badge, walking with Mira
items.why: Signed in and escorted. That's the process working.

items.label: Someone slips through the side door right behind you
items.why: Tailgating skips every check. Ask them to badge in or go to reception.

items.label: A parcel left with reception for collection
items.why: Normal delivery handling.

items.label: A visitor asks for the Wi-Fi password and the VPN address
items.why: Network details help an attacker get inside. Send them to IT.

rounds.explain: The question is always: did this person go through reception?

rounds.prompt: Zoe, a colleague you know, is at the door without her badge.
lines: I left my badge at home, can you just let me in?

options.text: Send her to reception for a day pass
Let her in: you know her
Lend her your badge
Ignore her

rounds.explain: Reception can check and issue a pass in a minute. The rule is the same for everyone, so nobody has to judge.

recap: Everyone shows a badge or signs in at reception, even if their hands are full.
Check 'X said it's fine' with X, not with the visitor.
Help genuine people too: direct them and walk them to reception.

sources.title: Guidelines on Information Security Practices for Government Entities

simulations.title: Money requests
intro: The most expensive scams don't steal passwords. They ask someone to send money.
Watch for the recipe: urgency, secrecy and a reason to skip the usual process.
And if money has already gone, every minute counts.

rounds.prompt: Tap every red flag in this email.

body: We're closing an acquisition. Please send ₹18,50,000 to our new legal partner [[deadline|before 4 PM today]].
[[secret|Keep this between us]] and [[skip|don't involve Finance yet]]. Details below.

regions.label: Sender address
regions.why: novacorp-exec.com isn't novacorp.com.

regions.label: Same-day deadline
regions.why: A hard deadline stops you checking.

regions.label: Secrecy
regions.why: Real payments don't need to be secret from colleagues.

regions.label: Skip Finance
regions.why: Skipping the process is the whole point of the scam.

regions.label: Greeting
regions.why: A normal greeting. Not a flag on its own.

rounds.explain: Urgency + secrecy + skipping the process = stop and verify.

rounds.prompt: BrightClean emails new bank details right before the monthly payment run. What's the right check?

options.text: Call BrightClean on the number in the contract
Reply to the email to confirm
Call the number in the email
Update the details: the email looks real

rounds.explain: Bank detail changes are confirmed by phone on a number you already have, never through the email that asks.

rounds.prompt: A WhatsApp call from "Mr. Hale (CFO)".

say: It's Hale. My phone broke, this is my new number.
A vendor payment of ₹4,80,000 is overdue and they're threatening to stop supply. Can you send it today?

choices.text: Sure, send me the account details.
choices.why: New number, urgency and a skipped process. The money would go straight to a fraudster.

choices.text: Please raise it in the finance portal. I'll confirm with you on your directory number.
choices.why: The portal and a call-back protect everyone, even if it really is him.

choices.text: Can you email me from your work address?

say: My laptop's with IT. Look, I'll take responsibility. Just send it.

choices.text: Okay, I'll send it.
choices.why: 'I'll take responsibility' doesn't make a payment safe. The process does.

choices.text: Then I'll call you on your directory number first.
choices.why: Right. A real CFO wants the process followed.

rounds.explain: Payments go through the finance portal with approval, whoever asks and however urgent.

rounds.prompt: Which address really belongs to BrightClean's accounts team?

options.text: accounts@bright-clean.in
options.note: The hyphen makes a different domain.

options.text: accounts@brightclean.in

rounds.explain: Fraudsters register near-identical vendor domains to slip into invoice threads.

rounds.prompt: Process it, or report it?

items.label: FIN-2291 in the finance portal, approved by the CFO
items.why: The normal process with approval attached.

items.label: "Our bank details have changed, effective immediately"
items.why: Bank changes must be confirmed by phone on the contract number.

items.label: "Buy ₹10,000 of gift cards for a client"
items.why: Gift cards are a favourite way to move stolen money.

items.label: Monthly invoice from a known vendor via the portal
items.detail: Same amount and account as usual
items.why: Nothing has changed and it uses the portal.

rounds.explain: Changes, urgency and new channels are your cue to verify.

rounds.prompt: You realise a payment you sent 20 minutes ago went to a fraudster. What do you do first?

options.text: Tell Finance and the bank straight away, and report it on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in
Wait until tomorrow to see if it bounces
Email the fraudster asking for the money back
Keep quiet and hope nobody notices

rounds.explain: Banks can sometimes freeze money if they hear quickly. 1930 is India's national helpline for financial cyber fraud.

recap: Urgency + secrecy + a skipped process = stop and verify.
Bank detail changes are confirmed by phone on the number you already have.
Paid a fraudster? Tell Finance and the bank at once and call 1930: speed matters.
